lessons.title: Rounding to the nearest place value
lessons.summary: Choose the closest multiple, round decimal places and show zeros after a carry.
lessons.objective: Choose the closest multiple, round decimal places and show zeros after a carry.
lessons.before: Identify ones, tens, tenths and hundredths. A decimal can be between two multiples of the place you are rounding to.
lessons.ideas:
To round to the nearest hundred, compare the two multiples of 100 around the number. For a positive value exactly halfway, choose the greater multiple.

Keep the requested decimal place. Use the next digit to decide if that place increases. One decimal place must still be visible when the last digit is zero.

Complete the whole-number places with zeros after rounding to tens, hundreds or thousands. For a negative number away from a halfway point, round its magnitude then restore the minus sign.
lessons.method:
Which multiple is nearest?

Rounding replaces a number with the closest value at a stated place. Mark the two possible results on a number line.

Which digit decides the rounded decimal?

Count places after the decimal point. The first place is tenths and the second is hundredths.

What happens with a carry or a negative number?

The digit 9 becomes a zero at that place when it carries into the next column. If the number is negative, compare distances to nearby multiples.
mistakes: Rounding to the nearest hundred is about distance to multiples of 100. It does not always mean moving up.
A carry can increase the ones and leave a zero in the tenths. Write the zero if the question asks for one decimal place.
On the negative side, the nearest value may be further left or further right. Keep the sign when you give the answer.

examples.title: Find the nearest multiple
examples.question: Round \(126\) to the nearest \(10\).
examples.solution:
The multiples of 10 on either side are \(120\) and \(130\).

\(126\) is \(6\) above \(120\) and \(4\) below \(130\).

The nearer multiple is \(130\).

examples.title: Round a halfway value
examples.question: Round \(2.815\) to two decimal places.
examples.solution:
The two nearest hundredths are \(2.81\) and \(2.82\).

\(2.815\) is exactly halfway between them. Its thousandths digit is 5.

For this positive halfway value keep the upper hundredth, \(2.82\).

examples.title: Carry into the next thousand
examples.question: Round \(4995\) to the nearest hundred.
examples.solution:
The hundreds digit is 9 and the tens digit is 9.

Rounding up carries from the hundreds into the thousands.

The correct multiple of one hundred is \(5000\).

lessons.title: Rounding to significant figures
lessons.summary: Count from the first non-zero digit and keep the right precision when zeros appear.
lessons.objective: Count from the first non-zero digit and keep the right precision when zeros appear.
lessons.before: Recognise the first non-zero digit in a whole number or decimal. Read the place immediately to the right of a chosen digit.
lessons.ideas:
Start counting significant figures there. Digits in places before that do not count. A zero in a later place can count.

When a carry changes the leading position, check the significant figures in the written answer again. For example, \(0.00996\) to two significant figures is \(0.010\).

The same number can round to different results under these two instructions. Check your final answer against the required unit and accuracy.
lessons.method:
Where do significant figures start?

Read left to right until you reach the first non-zero digit. Its position shows the approximate size of the number.

Why do some zeros count and others stay as placeholders?

Leading zeros show the position of a small number. A zero after the first significant digit can record accuracy.

Which kind of accuracy is the question asking for?

Underline the instruction. Count decimal places from the point and significant figures from the first non-zero digit.
mistakes: Starting at the decimal point works for decimal places. Significant figures start at the first non-zero digit.
Dropping the last zero in \(0.010\) would leave only one significant figure visible.
Two decimal places and two significant figures often need different digits even when there is only one digit before the point.

examples.title: Keep the place value of a large number
examples.question: Give the value of \(18213\) correct to 2 significant figures.
examples.solution:
The first significant digit is the leftmost non-zero digit.

The 2 significant figures bring you to the thousands place. Check the next digit.

Replace remaining whole-number places with zeros and give \(18000\).

examples.title: Find the first non-zero digit in a small number
examples.question:
Which option gives \(0.003527\) to three significant figures?

A. \(0.00353\)   B. \(0.004\)   C. \(0.0035\)
examples.solution:
Ignore the zeros that come before the first non-zero digit when counting significant figures.

Count three digits from the first non-zero digit. Use the fourth significant digit to round.

Keep the leading zeros in their places and write \(0.00353\).

examples.title: Compare decimal places with significant figures
examples.question:
Round \(4.02374\) to two decimal places and to two significant figures. Which pair gives the answers in that order?

A. \(4.02\) and \(4.0\)   B. \(4.0\) and \(4.02\)   C. \(4.03\) and \(4.0\)   D. \(4.02\) and \(4.1\)
examples.solution:
For decimal places, count two places after the point. The result is \(4.02\).

For significant figures, start with the ones digit 4. The second significant place is the tenths.

The ordered pair of answers is \(4.02\) and \(4.0\).

lessons.title: Estimating calculations without a calculator
lessons.summary: Round inputs to convenient values, keep the operations and check the size of the result.
lessons.objective: Round inputs to convenient values, keep the operations and check the size of the result.
lessons.before: Round to one significant figure. Identify the operations and anything grouped by brackets, a fraction bar or a root.
lessons.ideas:
If the question asks for one significant figure, round each input separately. Use \(\approx\) for the step where you replace an expression by an estimate.

Round a non-zero small divisor by significant figures, rather than changing it to zero by rounding to a whole number. If a rounded denominator still becomes zero, the proposed estimate does not work.

Show enough working to see why an answer close to 120 is plausible when the estimate is 120. An answer near 12 or 1200 deserves another check.
lessons.method:
When does the rounding happen?

An estimate is an approximate answer that you can work out quickly. Replace the original inputs by nearby values before calculating.

How do I keep the calculation sensible?

Use the same operations in the same order as the original. The fraction bar groups the whole numerator and the whole denominator.

How can I estimate a root and check the scale?

Keep the entire rounded group inside a square root. Use the estimate to spot a misplaced decimal point or an order-of-operations error.
mistakes: Rounding the exact answer afterward does not show how the estimate was obtained.
A zero in the ones place does not mean the decimal has no significant digits.
An estimate can flag a possible error. It does not prove that an exact answer is correct.

examples.title: Round both addends before adding
examples.question: Estimate \(28.7+1.81\) by rounding each value to one significant figure.

examples.title: Keep an estimated divisor non-zero
examples.question: Estimate \(\frac{0.408}{0.21}\) by rounding each value to one significant figure.
examples.solution:
The rounded numerator is \(0.4\) and the rounded denominator is \(0.2\).

The denominator has one significant figure even though its whole-number digit is zero.

Calculate \(\frac{0.4}{0.2}\), which equals \(2\).

examples.title: Estimate before evaluating a square root
examples.question: Round each number inside \(\sqrt{4.18\times 8.80}\) to one significant figure. Then estimate the root.
examples.solution:
The rounded values are \(4\) and \(9\).

Multiply inside the root first. The rounded product is \(36\).

The positive square root is \(6\).

lessons.title: Choosing useful accuracy in context
lessons.summary: Decide whether a real situation needs a nearest value, an extra container or a count of complete groups.
lessons.objective: Decide whether a real situation needs a nearest value, an extra container or a count of complete groups.
lessons.before: Read the units and the wording of the question. Look for a direction such as minimum needed, complete groups or nearest penny.
lessons.ideas:
Round up when every item needs a place and another group may be partly full. Round down when only complete items or groups count.

Record a price to the nearest penny using two decimal places in pounds. If the requested final position is zero, keep it visible.

Unless told otherwise, Cambridge 0580 uses three significant figures for non-exact numerical answers and one decimal place for angles in degrees.
lessons.method:
When should a result move up or down?

A quotient can leave a remainder. Ask what the remainder means in the situation before choosing the whole-number answer.

Which position matches the units?

Choose a place that answers the question in the required units. One centimetre is one hundredth of a metre.

What do I report when the question gives no extra rule?

Keep the calculation accurate until the end. Use estimates early only when a question asks for a rough result or you want to check the scale.
mistakes: Rounding to the nearest whole number can undercount the containers you need or overcount the items you can cut.
Keep the units in the result. Copying the same digits with a different unit changes the stated quantity.
Rounding intermediate results can shift the final answer. Keep the unrounded result when it feeds another part.

examples.title: Round up when every item needs a place
examples.question: A studio packs 21 model boats. Each crate holds at most 4 boats. What is the minimum number of crates needed?
examples.solution:
5 full crates hold 20 boats.

There are 1 boats left. They need one more crate even though it will not be full.

The minimum is 6 crates.

examples.title: Report money to the nearest penny
examples.question:
A price calculation gives £\(3.2975\) before rounding. Which option records the price correctly to the nearest penny?

A. \(3.30\)   B. \(3.3\)   C. \(3.29\)   D. \(3.31\)
examples.solution:
The pounds and pence display needs two digits after the decimal point.

The hundredths digit rounds up, because the next digit is 7. The carry gives \(3.30\).

The price is £\(3.30\).

examples.title: Report an angle using the exam convention
examples.question:
A calculator gives an angle of \(6.87293^\circ\). The question gives no other required accuracy. Which displayed value follows the 0580 convention?

A. \(6.9\)   B. \(6.87\)   C. \(7\)
examples.solution:
In 0580, use one decimal place for a non-exact angle in degrees unless the question specifies otherwise.

The first decimal place is the tenths position. Use the next digit to round.

Report \(6.9^\circ\).
